messages.content: {"success": true, "name": "browser-console-ui-automation", "description": "Drive web UIs by injecting JS via browser_console.", "tags": ["browser-automation", "react", "prosemirror", "ui-automation", "browser-console"], "related_skills": ["mcp-browser-automation", "js-rendered-site-extraction", "inspecting-hermes-desktop-dom"], "content": "--- name: browser-console-ui-automation description: Drive web UIs by injecting JS via browser_console. version: 1.0.0 author: Hermes license: MIT metadata: hermes: tags: [browser-automation, react, prosemirror, ui-automation, browser-console] related_skills: [mcp-browser-automation, js-rendered-site-extraction, inspecting-hermes-desktop-dom] --- # Driving a web UI via `browser_console` JS injection ## When to Use - The target app is a modern JS SPA (React/ProseMirror/Vue) and **snapshot+ref clicking is fragile or too expensive** — a large board/table snapshot can cost ~15k chars per read. - You need to fill, submit, or read a control that has no stable ref, or that is rendered in a **portal** outside its visual parent. - You need to perform many similar actions and want to batch them in code. Do **not** reach for this when refs work fine — `browser_click` / `browser_type` on a stable `@eN` ref is simpler and self-documenting. Use this when refs are unstable, expensive, or the element is unreachable by scoping. Full worked case study (Trello): `references/trello-case-study.md`. ## 0. First prove you are in the app, not on a loading or login screen A successful `browser_navigate` and a "loading… [100%]" indicator are **not** evidence of a usable session. A WhatsApp Web load reported `Carregando conversas [8%] → [35%] → [69%] → [100%]` and then settled on the **QR login screen** — zero controls to automate. Probe authoritative DOM markers in one call, and **poll** instead of sleeping a fixed time (the SPA mounts after `readyState: complete`): ```js JSON.stringify({ readyState: document.readyState, paneSide: !!document.querySelector('#pane-side'), rows: document.querySelectorAll('[role="row"][data-testid^="list-item-"]').length, qr: !!document.querySelector('canvas[aria-label], div[data-ref]'), sess: Object.keys(localStorage).filter(k => k.startsWith('wds')).length }) ``` - Decide from the **app's own chrome** (its side pane, list rows, search input) and from the app's **session keys in `localStorage`** — never from progress text or `readyState`. - A native-browser runtime is its **own profile**: the user being logged into Chrome, or into another app's browser, says nothing about this session. - `browser_snapshot` returning `element_count: 0` is **not** proof the page is empty — an SPA mid-mount looks like that. Probe by JS before concluding. **Authentication is the user's step, not yours.** You cannot log in for them; when the probe says "not logged in", stop and hand over the path that actually works remotely: - A QR rendered in the page **refreshes on a short cycle (~20s)** — a screenshot sent to the user arrives already expired. Share the screenshot only to point at which window to look at, and tell them to scan from the live window. - Prefer the app's **code-based pairing** alternative ("connect with phone number" → an 8-digit code typed on the phone): one copyable code beats a QR that changes before the user looks at it. Read the code out of the DOM and dictate it. - Leave "keep me signed in on this browser" checked when offered — otherwise the user re-pairs on every profile restart. ## 1. Know your evaluator's powers and limits `browser_console` **awaits promises** — `(async () => { ... })()` with `await` and a local `sleep` works, which is what makes UI automation viable at all. ```js const sleep = ms => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms)); ``` **It also has a controller timeout.** Three `sleep(3000)` in one call produced `WorkstationBrowserError: Hermes Browser controller request timed out`. Keep each call to **~3–4s of accumulated waiting**; split long jobs across calls and append results to a workspace file if the job is big. **A call that times out is not a mutation that failed.** `… timed out after dispatch` means the request *left* — the page-side work often completes anyway (a card description was saved by a call that reported a timeout). Read the state back before repeating anything: a blind retry of a mutation that already landed duplicates or overwrites it. **To beat the timeout on slow per-item work, stop waiting inside the page.** Kick the work off, return immediately, and poll from later calls. Chain each item onto a page-global promise and collect per-item results in a page-global array: ```js window.__done = window.__done || []; window.__q = (window.__q || Promise.resolve()).then(() => __fill(item, payload).then(r => window.__done.push(r))); 'QUEUED'; // returns in milliseconds ``` Read `window.__done.length` / `String(window.__done)` in cheap follow-up calls, and sleep in the **shell** between polls (`terminal: sleep 20`) — an in-page wait loop is subject to the same controller timeout, so it cannot be the fix. ### Call hygiene for long per-item loops Each rule below cost real round-trips when ignored. - **Pair the action call and the read call in ONE assistant turn.** A `browser_navigate` (or a `location.assign` console call) followed in the same turn by the `browser_console` read is executed in order, so a loop over N pages advances one item per turn instead of two. Have the read return `location.pathname` together with the expected identifier, so a read that arrived before the navigation is visible at once instead of being mistaken for an empty page. - **Vary the expression text between iterations of the same call.** A loop that issues a byte-identical tool call repeatedly can trip the mutation-approval gate and hand the turn to the user mid-collection. Embed the current target id (or a counter) in the expression — same effect, distinct text. - **Wait on a readiness token, not a clock.** Poll the page for the app's own label (`document.body.innerText.indexOf('Visualiza') >= 0 && length > 90`) in a short loop of ~450 ms steps; a fixed sleep either wastes the budget or reads a half-rendered panel. - **Keep each write-argument small when relaying page text to disk through your own tool calls.** One item (post, row, record) per file, roughly 1 KB, is the safe unit. A single oversized argument (~3 KB was enough) can arrive *truncated* and be written without any error — a silently corrupt file. Never conclude from "the write succeeded". Close the loop by parsing every file with a script and asserting the count, id uniqueness, and the presence of the expected markers before any downstream step consumes them. - **Order the fallbacks for getting data out of a page:** in-page accumulator printed in the console result (always works) → shell/clipboard bridge for actual files → a local HTTP sink. A page's CSP applies to page-side `fetch`, so an https origin posting to `http://127.0.0.1:...` is typically refused, and a page-initiated download raises a native dialog that page JS cannot dismiss. When either route stalls, stop after one probe and take the accumulator path — do not debug the transport. **Exception, verified:** CSP gates page-side `fetch` only. A **top-level navigation** to `http://127.0.0.1:/sink?n=file.txt&d=` carries the payload in the query string and is *not* subject to `connect-src` — that is the byte-exact route **out** of a page (§8), and a local page writing `window.name` before `location.replace(appUrl)` is the byte-exact route **in**. - **Keep an injected helper alive by navigating inside the app.** Load the list/board once, inject `window.__fill`, then move item to item by clicking the item's own anchor (`a[href^="/c/"]`) — an SPA transition keeps the injected globals. A top-level `browser_navigate` reloads the document and silently drops them, so every item then costs a fresh injection. - **Relaying a big payload *into* the page: compress it and make it self-checking.** gzip+base64 cuts the console argument ~3×, but the real value is that corruption cannot pass silently — `atob` throws `InvalidCharacterError` on a mangled base64 and the decompressor throws on mangled bytes, so a bad relay fails loudly instead of writing wrong text. After the write, assert the control's length/sentinel and read the server state back. - **A `handoff_requested` result is a stop, not a retry loop.** When the mutation gate fires, the call did *not* run. Short single-purpose expressions pass where long compound ones (several DOM globals in one `JSON.stringify`) trip it. Retry the same intent once with a simpler expression; if it persists, stop and ask the human to confirm the pending handoff — never route around it with another tool. **But the retry is itself what kills the confirmation:** each gated call supersedes the previous request and mints a fresh `handoff_id` (a superseded call surfaces as `CANCELLED`), so a retry loop leaves the human nothing stable to approve and never terminates — the id you just showed them is already dead. For a gated navigation there is no simpler-expression retry at all: name the live `handoff_id` and its target, end the turn, and wait for the approval. Bulk mutation raises the odds, so keep batches small and verify between them. While the gate is closed, switch to read-only work (read the app's own edit history, gather evidence, draft the plan) instead of re-issuing mutations — **navigations count as mutations** for this gate, so a retry loop of `browser_navigate` gets refused too. ### Persist confirmed items to disk, batch by batch A page-global accumulator (`window.__done`) is a **transport, not a record**: it dies with the tab, and once the mutation gate closes or the context is compacted the only list of what landed is the conversation. Hospital Estadual de Jataí promove mais uma edição do Programa Nascer HEJ Iniciativa oferece orientação gratuita e visita guiada à maternidade para gestantes no último trimestre O Hospital Estadual de Jataí Dr. Serafim de Carvalho (HEJ) realiza nesta quinta-feira, 15 de outubro, às 8h, mais uma edição do Programa Nascer HEJ. O encontro acontece no auditório da unidade e é voltado para gestantes a partir da 30ª semana de gestação e seus familiares. Criada em 2023, em parceria entre a Secretaria de Estado da Saúde de Goiás (SES-GO) e a Secretaria Municipal de Saúde de Jataí, a iniciativa busca ampliar o acesso à informação, reduzir medos e ansiedade diante do parto e aproximar as gestantes da equipe assistencial. A programação será conduzida por equipe multiprofissional, composta por profissionais de psicologia, enfermagem, serviço social, fisioterapia e doulas, com abordagem irá abordar temas como os tipos de parto, benefícios do aleitamento materno, primeiros cuidados com o recém-nascido, direitos da gestante e orientações para o puerpério. O roteiro inclui, ainda, visita guiada nas dependências da maternidade, com passagem pela sala de parto e pela enfermaria, para que as participantes conheçam a estrutura e entendam o fluxo de atendimento no nascimento. Referência em saúde materno-infantil, o HEJ possui a certificação Hospital Amigo da Criança (IHAC), concedida pela Organização Mundial da Saúde (OMS) e pelo Ministério da Saúde, voltada à promoção do aleitamento materno, e o Prêmio Dr. Pinotti – Hospital Amigo da Mulher, que reconhece o atendimento humanizado à mulher em todo o ciclo gestacional. Serviço: Programa Nascer HEJ Data: quinta-feira, 15 de outubro, às 8h Local: auditório do Hospital Estadual de Jataí Dr. Serafim de Carvalho Endereço: Rua Joaquim Caetano, nº 1876 - Divino Espírito Santo, Jataí-Goiás

Hospital Estadual de Jataí promove mais uma edição do Programa Nascer HEJ Iniciativa oferece orientação gratuita e visita guiada à maternidade para gestantes no último trimestre O Hospital Estadual de Jataí Dr. Serafim de Carvalho (HEJ) realiza nesta quinta-feira, 15 de outubro, às 8h, mais uma edição do Programa Nascer HEJ. O encontro acontece no auditório da unidade e é voltado para gestantes a partir da 30ª semana de gestação e seus familiares. Criada em 2023, em parceria entre a Secretaria de Estado da Saúde de Goiás (SES-GO) e a Secretaria Municipal de Saúde de Jataí, a iniciativa busca ampliar o acesso à informação, reduzir medos e ansiedade diante do parto e aproximar as gestantes da equipe assistencial. A programação será conduzida por equipe multiprofissional, composta por profissionais de psicologia, enfermagem, serviço social, fisioterapia e doulas, com abordagem irá abordar temas como os tipos de parto, benefícios do aleitamento materno, primeiros cuidados com o recém-nascido, direitos da gestante e orientações para o puerpério. O roteiro inclui, ainda, visita guiada nas dependências da maternidade, com passagem pela sala de parto e pela enfermaria, para que as participantes conheçam a estrutura e entendam o fluxo de atendimento no nascimento. Referência em saúde materno-infantil, o HEJ possui a certificação Hospital Amigo da Criança (IHAC), concedida pela Organização Mundial da Saúde (OMS) e pelo Ministério da Saúde, voltada à promoção do aleitamento materno, e o Prêmio Dr. Pinotti – Hospital Amigo da Mulher, que reconhece o atendimento humanizado à mulher em todo o ciclo gestacional. Serviço: Programa Nascer HEJ Data: quinta-feira, 15 de outubro, às 8h Local: auditório do Hospital Estadual de Jataí Dr. Serafim de Carvalho Endereço: Rua Joaquim Caetano, nº 1876 - Divino Espírito Santo, Jataí-Goiás

Do **not** reach for this when refs work fine — `browser_click` / `browser_type` on a stable `@eN` ref is simpler and self-documenting. Use this when refs are unstable, expensive, or the element is unreachable by scoping. Full worked case study (Trello): `references/trello-case-study.md`. ## 0. First prove you are in the app, not on a loading or login screen A successful `browser_navigate` and a "loading… [100%]" indicator are **not** evidence of a usable session. A WhatsApp Web load reported `Carregando conversas [8%] → [35%] → [69%] → [100%]` and then settled on the **QR login screen** — zero controls to automate. Probe authoritative DOM markers in one call, and **poll** instead of sleeping a fixed time (the SPA mounts after `readyState: complete`): ```js JSON.stringify({ readyState: document.readyState, paneSide: !!document.querySelector('#pane-side'), rows: document.querySelectorAll('[role="row"][data-testid^="list-item-"]').length, qr: !!document.querySelector('canvas[aria-label], div[data-ref]'), sess: Object.keys(localStorage).filter(k => k.startsWith('wds')).length }) ``` - Decide from the **app's own chrome** (its side pane, list rows, search input) and from the app's **session keys in `localStorage`** — never from progress text or `readyState`. - A native-browser runtime is its **own profile**: the user being logged into Chrome, or into another app's browser, says nothing about this session. - `browser_snapshot` returning `element_count: 0` is **not** proof the page is empty — an SPA mid-mount looks like that. Probe by JS before concluding. **Authentication is the user's step, not yours.** You cannot log in for them; when the probe says "not logged in", stop and hand over the path that actually works remotely: - A QR rendered in the page **refreshes on a short cycle (~20s)** — a screenshot sent to the user arrives already expired. Share the screenshot only to point at which window to look at, and tell them to scan from the live window. - Prefer the app's **code-based pairing** alternative ("connect with phone number" → an 8-digit code typed on the phone): one copyable code beats a QR that changes before the user looks at it. Read the code out of the DOM and dictate it. - Leave "keep me signed in on this browser" checked when offered — otherwise the user re-pairs on every profile restart. ## 1. Know your evaluator's powers and limits `browser_console` **awaits promises** — `(async () => { ... })()` with `await` and a local `sleep` works, which is what makes UI automation viable at all. ```js const sleep = ms => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms)); ``` **It also has a controller timeout.** Three `sleep(3000)` in one call produced `WorkstationBrowserError: Hermes Browser controller request timed out`. Keep each call to **~3–4s of accumulated waiting**; split long jobs across calls and append results to a workspace file if the job is big. **A call that times out is not a mutation that failed.** `… timed out after dispatch` means the request *left* — the page-side work often completes anyway (a card description was saved by a call that reported a timeout). Read the state back before repeating anything: a blind retry of a mutation that already landed duplicates or overwrites it. **To beat the timeout on slow per-item work, stop waiting inside the page.** Kick the work off, return immediately, and poll from later calls. Chain each item onto a page-global promise and collect per-item results in a page-global array: ```js window.__done = window.__done || []; window.__q = (window.__q || Promise.resolve()).then(() => __fill(item, payload).then(r => window.__done.push(r))); 'QUEUED'; // returns in milliseconds ``` Read `window.__done.length` / `String(window.__done)` in cheap follow-up calls, and sleep in the **shell** between polls (`terminal: sleep 20`) — an in-page wait loop is subject to the same controller timeout, so it cannot be the fix. ### Call hygiene for long per-item loops Each rule below cost real round-trips when ignored. - **Pair the action call and the read call in ONE assistant turn.** A `browser_navigate` (or a `location.assign` console call) followed in the same turn by the `browser_console` read is executed in order, so a loop over N pages advances one item per turn instead of two. Have the read return `location.pathname` together with the expected identifier, so a read that arrived before the navigation is visible at once instead of being mistaken for an empty page. - **Vary the expression text between iterations of the same call.** A loop that issues a byte-identical tool call repeatedly can trip the mutation-approval gate and hand the turn to the user mid-collection. Embed the current target id (or a counter) in the expression — same effect, distinct text. - **Wait on a readiness token, not a clock.** Poll the page for the app's own label (`document.body.innerText.indexOf('Visualiza') >= 0 && length > 90`) in a short loop of ~450 ms steps; a fixed sleep either wastes the budget or reads a half-rendered panel. - **Keep each write-argument small when relaying page text to disk through your own tool calls.** One item (post, row, record) per file, roughly 1 KB, is the safe unit. A single oversized argument (~3 KB was enough) can arrive *truncated* and be written without any error — a silently corrupt file. Never conclude from "the write succeeded". Close the loop by parsing every file with a script and asserting the count, id uniqueness, and the presence of the expected markers before any downstream step consumes them. - **Order the fallbacks for getting data out of a page:** in-page accumulator printed in the console result (always works) → shell/clipboard bridge for actual files → a local HTTP sink. A page's CSP applies to page-side `fetch`, so an https origin posting to `http://127.0.0.1:...` is typically refused, and a page-initiated download raises a native dialog that page JS cannot dismiss. When either route stalls, stop after one probe and take the accumulator path — do not debug the transport. **Exception, verified:** CSP gates page-side `fetch` only. A **top-level navigation** to `http://127.0.0.1:/sink?n=file.txt&d=` carries the payload in the query string and is *not* subject to `connect-src` — that is the byte-exact route **out** of a page (§8), and a local page writing `window.name` before `location.replace(appUrl)` is the byte-exact route **in**. - **Keep an injected helper alive by navigating inside the app.** Load the list/board once, inject `window.__fill`, then move item to item by clicking the item's own anchor (`a[href^="/c/"]`) — an SPA transition keeps the injected globals. A top-level `browser_navigate` reloads the document and silently drops them, so every item then costs a fresh injection. - **Relaying a big payload *into* the page: compress it and make it self-checking.** gzip+base64 cuts the console argument ~3×, but the real value is that corruption cannot pass silently — `atob` throws `InvalidCharacterError` on a mangled base64 and the decompressor throws on mangled bytes, so a bad relay fails loudly instead of writing wrong text. After the write, assert the control's length/sentinel and read the server state back. - **A `handoff_requested` result is a stop, not a retry loop.** When the mutation gate fires, the call did *not* run. Short single-purpose expressions pass where long compound ones (several DOM globals in one `JSON.stringify`) trip it. Retry the same intent once with a simpler expression; if it persists, stop and ask the human to confirm the pending handoff — never route around it with another tool. **But the retry is itself what kills the confirmation:** each gated call supersedes the previous request and mints a fresh `handoff_id` (a superseded call surfaces as `CANCELLED`), so a retry loop leaves the human nothing stable to approve and never terminates — the id you just showed them is already dead. For a gated navigation there is no simpler-expression retry at all: name the live `handoff_id` and its target, end the turn, and wait for the approval. Bulk mutation raises the odds, so keep batches small and verify between them. While the gate is closed, switch to read-only work (read the app's own edit history, gather evidence, draft the plan) instead of re-issuing mutations — **navigations count as mutations** for this gate, so a retry loop of `browser_navigate` gets refused too. ### Persist confirmed items to disk, batch by batch A page-global accumulator (`window.__done`) is a **transport, not a record**: it dies with the tab, and once the mutation gate closes or the context is compacted the only list of what landed is the conversation. A long run can end with dozens of confirmed writes and no way to enumerate them. - After every batch, write the confirmed pairs (item id + status) to a file on disk **before** queueing the next batch — one line per item, append-only. - Recover the remaining work from that file plus the app's own read endpoint (`GET …?fields=desc`), never from your recollection of the conversation. - If you cannot enumerate the remaining items from disk plus one read, the run is not resumable — stop and close that gap before writing anything else. **A failed compressed relay is regenerated, not patched.** `InvalidCharacterError` from `atob`, or a decompressor fault, means the base64 was mangled *in transit* (a long argument relayed through tool calls), not that the content is wrong. Re-run the generator script to emit a fresh payload and re-queue that item; emit the payload as one line from a script and copy it verbatim — never hand-assemble or hand-repair base64. **Verified:** synchronous `XMLHttpRequest` (`x.open(method, url, false)`) works inside the page and is the most direct way to read authenticated state. ## 2. 107|### Call hygiene for long per-item loops
108|
109|Each rule below cost real round-trips when ignored.
110|
111|- **Pair the action call and the read call in ONE assistant turn.** A
112|  `browser_navigate` (or a `location.assign` console call) followed in the same turn
113|  by the `browser_console` read is executed in order, so a loop over N pages advances
114|  one item per turn instead of two. Have the read return `location.pathname` together
115|  with the expected identifier, so a read that arrived before the navigation is visible
116|  at once instead of being mistaken for an empty page.
117|- **Vary the expression text between iterations of the same call.** A loop that issues a
118|  byte-identical tool call repeatedly can trip the mutation-approval gate and hand the
119|  turn to the user mid-collection. Embed the current target id (or a counter) in the
120|  expression — same effect, distinct text.
121|- **Wait on a readiness token, not a clock.** Poll the page for the app's own label
122|  (`document.body.innerText.indexOf('Visualiza') >= 0 && length > 90`) in a short loop of
123|  ~450 ms steps; a fixed sleep either wastes the budget or reads a half-rendered panel.
124|- **Keep each write-argument small when relaying page text to disk through your own tool
125|  calls.** One item (post, row, record) per file, roughly 1 KB, is the safe unit. A single
126|  oversized argument (~3 KB was enough) can arrive *truncated* and be written without any
127|  error — a silently corrupt file. Never conclude from "the write succeeded". Close the
128|  loop by parsing every file with a script and asserting the count, id uniqueness, and the
129|  presence of the expected markers before any downstream step consumes them.
130|- **Order the fallbacks for getting data out of a page:** in-page accumulator printed in
131|  the console result (always works) → shell/clipboard bridge for actual files → a local
132|  HTTP sink. A page's CSP applies to page-side `fetch`, so an https origin posting to
133|  `http://127.0.0.1:...` is typically refused, and a page-initiated download raises a
134|  native dialog that page JS cannot dismiss. When either route stalls, stop after one
135|  probe and take the accumulator path — do not debug the transport. **Exception, verified:**
136|  CSP gates page-side `fetch` only. A **top-level navigation** to
137|  `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/sink?n=file.txt&d=<base64url>` carries the payload in the
138|  query string and is *not* subject to `connect-src` — that is the byte-exact route
139|  **out** of a page (§8), and a local page writing `window.name` before

143|  anchor (`a[href^="/c/<id>"]`) — an SPA transition keeps the injected globals. A
